opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think it gets at something people often get wrong when they first start using these tools. The instinct is to treat the agent like a senior engineer who's been on your team for two years, and it's just not that, at least not out of the box. It's more like a really talented new hire on their first day. They're smart, they're fast, they know a ton about programming in general, but they don't know why your team made the weird architectural decision three years ago, or which module everybody's afraid to touch.

So the way I think about delegation is a few things. First, scope the task so the context it needs is discoverable. The CLI can read your repo, run commands, grep around, run your tests. If the information it needs actually lives in the code, it's surprisingly good at finding it. Where it struggles is when the important context lives in someone's head or in a Slack thread somewhere. So the tasks I hand off most confidently are ones where the "truth" is in the codebase: fix this failing test, add this endpoint following the pattern of these other three, refactor this function and make sure everything still passes.

Second, you can close a lot of that gap by just writing things down. Having an AGENTS.md or similar file in the repo that says, here's how we run tests, here's our style, here are the gotchas, goes a really long way. And honestly, it's good hygiene for human engineers too. A lot of what makes a codebase agent-friendly is the same stuff that makes it new-hire-friendly.

Third, lean on verification. The thing that makes delegation work isn't that the model gets it right the first time. It's that there's a tight loop where it can check its own work. If you have good tests, linters, type checking, the agent can iterate against those signals. If your repo has no tests, you're asking it to work blind, and you'll be doing much more of the checking yourself.

And then finally, I think about it in terms of the cost of being wrong. For things that are easy to review and easy to revert, I'll give it a lot of rope and just look at the diff. For things that are subtle or high-stakes, I'll break it into smaller steps, or use it more as a pair programmer where I'm steering as we go.

So the lack of context is real, but it's less a fundamental limitation and more something you design around. And as these models get better at exploring a codebase on their own, that gap keeps shrinking.

r001.rationale: It describes Codex as a new hire without project history, says it struggles when context is undocumented, and recommends smaller, guided steps for subtle or high-stakes work.

r002.rationale: It recommends scoping tasks and breaking high-stakes work into smaller steps, but does not clearly recommend delegating intern-sized chunks of work.

r003.rationale: It says the CLI can explore the repository by reading code, running commands, grepping, and running tests.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the most interesting questions about how you use these tools well, because the model walks in cold. It doesn't have the years of context you've built up about why things are structured the way they are, what the weird edge cases are, which parts of the codebase are load-bearing and which parts are scaffolding.

The way I think about it is a lot like onboarding a very capable new engineer who's going to work on your team for a single afternoon. You would never just say "go fix the flaky test" and walk away. You'd point them at the relevant directory, tell them the conventions, tell them what not to touch, and you'd scope the task so they can actually succeed without needing to understand the whole system. Codex is similar. The quality of the output is very correlated with how well you scope and ground the task up front.

In practice, a few things matter a lot. One is that the model is actually pretty good at building context for itself if you let it. It'll read files, grep around, run the tests. So part of delegating well is giving it the entry points and letting it do that exploration rather than trying to stuff everything into the prompt yourself. The second is that the codebase can carry a lot of that context for you. Good READMEs, an AGENTS.md file that explains how the repo is laid out and how to run things, consistent conventions. That stuff was always good practice, but now it has a very concrete payoff because the agent reads it every time.

And then the third thing is just being honest about which tasks are a good fit. Something that's well-specified and verifiable, where there's a test you can run or a clear definition of done, delegates really well. Something that depends on a lot of tacit knowledge about product intent or on taste, those are the tasks where I still want to be in the loop, or at least I want to break them into smaller pieces where the ambiguity is reduced.

I'd also say my own behavior has shifted. I spend more time now thinking about how to describe a task crisply and less time thinking about how to implement it. And that's actually a skill. The people who get the most out of these tools are the ones who've gotten good at that decomposition, at writing down the context they have in their heads in a way that another agent, human or model, can act on.

r001.rationale: The response says Codex starts without project-specific context and recommends keeping humans involved in tasks that depend on tacit knowledge or product intent.

r002.rationale: It recommends scoping tasks so the agent can succeed in a short stint and breaking ambiguous work into smaller pieces.

r003.rationale: It says Codex can build context by reading files, using grep, and running tests to explore the codebase.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a question of how much context a task requires and how easily I can verify the result. If I can give Codex a well-scoped task, point it at the relevant parts of the codebase, and tell it what success looks like, that’s a pretty good candidate for delegation.

The harder cases are where the request sounds simple, but there’s a lot of implicit knowledge behind it—why we made a particular architectural decision, or which behavior another service depends on. You have to make that context explicit, or stay more involved.

So I’d start with a smaller task, look at the diff, run the tests, and build up from there. The goal isn’t to write a prompt that explains the entire codebase. It’s to give it enough context to do the particular job, with a feedback loop that lets you catch misunderstandings.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks with substantial implicit project knowledge are harder and that the context must be made explicit or the user should stay more involved, conveying limits on delegating complex work.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with a smaller, well-scoped task, but does not clearly recommend work chunks sized for an intern.

r003.rationale: It does not identify ordinary command-line tools as how Codex CLI explores the codebase.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that you’re not delegating the same way you would to someone who’s been working in your codebase for six months. You have to give it a task where it can acquire the context it needs, and you have to be clear about what success looks like.

So I might point it at a particular part of the codebase, describe the behavior I want, and give it a way to check its work. And sometimes the first task is just, “Go understand how this works and explain what you’d change.” That gives me a chance to catch a misunderstanding before it starts making changes.

Then, as I get confidence in its understanding and its ability to verify the result, I can delegate something larger. The question is less, “Does it already know my whole codebase?” and more, “Can it find the relevant context, and can I tell whether it did the task correctly?”

r001.rationale: It says Codex must first acquire context and that larger tasks should wait until confidence grows, but it does not clearly connect its lack of project-specific experience to limits on trusting it with complex, context-heavy tasks.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting with a scoped task and expanding later, but does not recommend delegating intern-sized chunks of work.

r003.rationale: It says Codex can find relevant context, but does not identify ordinary command-line tools as the means for exploring the codebase.
